title: Audit custody envelopes: automated WORM escrow and residency-aware retention enforcement
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: Build an end-to-end mechanism that packages admin activity (admin actions, access events, config changes) into a verifiable "custody envelope", immutably stores envelopes in WORM-backed escrow, and enforces per-customer/data-residency retention policies with automated reporting and integrity proofs. This ticket implements the runtime producer, escrow sink, and orchestration for residency-aware retention lifecycles.

Context and motivation:
- Customers in regulated industries require tamper-evident archives of admin activity with proof of retention and per-region residency guarantees.
- Existing audit capture is high-fidelity but stored in mutable indices and logs that are unsuitable for long-term legal/regulatory evidence.
- We must provide automated exports (escrow) that preserve chain-of-custody, support legal hold, and enable auditors to verify integrity without exposing raw plaintext to operators.

Scope of work:
1) Custody envelope format and manifest: define manifest schema that bundles a compressed audit slice (time window), envelope metadata (customer, residency, retention policy, sequence range), cryptographic digest(s) (SHA-256 per-file + overall Merkle root), and KMS/HSM-signed envelope header. Envelopes are JSONL-compatible to support incremental verification.
2) Escrow sink: implement an append-only escrow writer that targets S3 Object Lock (Compliance mode) in region-specific buckets and an on-premises WORM appliance for Private deployments. Writes must be atomic per-envelope and provide a durable write confirmation to callers.
3) Residency mapping: route envelope writes to the customer's residency bucket based on account metadata. Include fallback routing rules for cross-region failover and a clear audit trail for any cross-region writes.
4) Retention enforcement: attach lifecycle manifests to envelopes and implement an orchestrator that enforces retention deletion windows, respects legal holds, and marks envelopes for secure purge.
5) Integrity proofs and verification APIs: compute Merkle roots per-envelope, store signed root attestations in the control plane, and provide a verification API endpoint for auditors to validate envelope authenticity and retention status.
6) Performance and backpressure: design an async batching producer that balances throughput with bounded memory and latency SLOs for admin APIs.
7) Observability and reporting: surface escrow metrics (envelope size, write latency, bucket residency, retention state), integrity verification success rates, and scheduled purge tasks in Console and on a compliance dashboard.

Design decisions and trade-offs considered:
- Synchronous vs asynchronous escrow writes: synchronous gives immediate evidence but increases latency of admin calls. We opted for a hybrid: a small immediate envelope (headers + digest) committed synchronously, with bulk payload uploaded asynchronously with guaranteed delivery and sequenced manifest updates.
- Full encryption at rest vs partial metadata indexing: payloads will be encrypted with customer-scoped KMS keys. We will index only opaque metadata fields (customer id, timestamp, residency, envelope id) in the control plane to enable search without decrypting contents.
- Merkle anchoring vs single-file digest: Merkle approach enables partial verification for large envelopes and incremental attestation; overhead is acceptable given smaller envelope sizes and improves auditor UX.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- 2025-03-18: Finalize envelope manifest schema and KMS signing format. (This ticket)
- 2025-03-25: Prototype escrow writer for S3 Object Lock (compliance mode) + local WORM shim for Private deployment testing.
- 2025-04-01: Integration of residency router and retention orchestrator; design Console views.
- 2025-04-08: End-to-end integration tests, retention lifecycle tests, and verification API.
- 2025-04-15: Beta rollout to five pilot customers and security review.

Security and compliance notes:
- KMS integration: use envelope keys derived from customer KMS key with HSM-backed signing for envelope headers. Store signed attestations in a write-once control plane store with immutable timestamps.
- Access controls: only a narrow service account may write to escrow buckets; retrieval APIs require audit-approved tokens and will only return verification artifacts or encrypted bundle download URLs.
- Tamper evidence: S3 Object Lock (Compliance mode) + stored signed Merkle roots provide tamper-evidence; for on-prem we will integrate with vendor WORM APIs and produce equivalent attestations.

Testing strategy:
- Unit tests for manifest generation, Merkle root calculation, KMS signing, and residency routing.
- Integration test harness that simulates high-rate admin activity (10K events/min) and validates bounded memory/latency and escrow delivery guarantees.
- End-to-end verification test where verifier service validates signatures and root against archived envelope.

Rollout and migration:
- Phase 1: New envelopes produced for all admin actions for pilot customers; old mutable audit entries are periodically snapshotted into envelopes when retention policy requires archival.
- Phase 2: Enable Object Lock buckets for regions in GA; provide migration tooling to bundle historical audit slices into custody envelopes.

Metrics and dashboard (initial):
- envelope_write_success_rate, envelope_write_latency_p95, envelope_delivery_lag, envelopes_per_customer_per_day, retention_purge_failures, verification_failure_rate

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Legal hold UX: should legal hold be per-envelope or per-customer? (PM leaning towards per-customer + per-case overrides)
- External timestamping: do we anchor Merkle roots to a public timestamping service for added non-repudiation? (Security requests feasibility analysis)

Deliverables:
- Envelope schema doc (Confluence), escrow writer (service + S3/WORM adapters), residency router updates, retention orchestrator, verification API, Console compliance dashboard views, end-to-end test suite, rollout runbook.
